newsitem.title: USA: CE Franklin aims to be oilfield superstore.
newsitem.headline: CE Franklin aims to be oilfield superstore.

text.p: CE Franklin Ltd, a wholesaler of supplies for oil and gas explorers, is looking to expand out of its Canadian home turf and become the McDonald's of oilfield services, the company's boss said in an interview.
Analysts say the playing field is ripe to be re-invented by the likes of CE Franklin, since the business is currently dominated by small 'mom and pop' operators.

"When Ray Kroc got into the hamburger business there were probably 100,000 hamburger shops," CE Franklin Chairman John Gilbank told Reuters in a recent interview, referring to the founder of McDonald's Corp.
"In the oilfield services business, there has been a lot of fragmentation," Gilbank said. "We believe that once we get the recipe right we can expand just about anywhere."

The company sells all the basics of oil drilling like pipes and pumps, but also provides services like taking care of other companies' inventories. Currently the company has 39 of its own warehouses, but runs another 45 for customers.

Its operations are concentrated in Canada's western oil provinces British Colombia, Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba, but CE Franklin has now also set up shop in Newfoundland on the Atlantic coast to service the giant offshore Hibernia field and others that may be developed in its wake.
Gilbank's recipe appears to be working, with a steadily rising stock price and earnings over the last several quarters.
Earlier this month, CE Frankln reported a solid jump in second quarter earnings, and Gilbank is confident the coast is clear for steady earnings growth given the loose structure of the industry.

CE Franklin shares, trading Thursday afternoon 1/16 higher at 6-1/8 on the American Stock Exchange, got a boost from the latest earnings report. The shares have also been rising steadily since last spring from levels just above $1 a share.

The company posted second quarter net income of C$1,621,175 million or $0.10 a share on sales of $83.7 million compared to sales of just C$97,401 or $0.01 a share on sales of $44.4 million in the same year-ago quarter.

While the results reflected an unusually active second quarter, Gilbank told analysts he was comfortable with estimates the company would earn $0.55 in the whole year, compared to $0.43 in all of 1996, a 25 percent gain.

To be sure, Gilbank's company is in a low margin business, just like the hugely-successful retailing giant Wallmart he invokes as he talks about CE Franklin and the competitive environment in which it operates.

But high volume, high productivity is the recipe Gilbank aims to perfect, and scanning the competititive enviroment, Gilroy said CE Franklin, already Canada's largest oilfield supplier, is alone in Canada in its aim to consolidate the oil services supplies industry.
"No one else has emerged in Canada. A 40 percent market share is realistic in Canada," Gilbank said, noting he sees steady growth in market share over the next several years.

The company now has a market share of around 13.5 percent, based on analyst estimates the company will post sales this year of $335 million, and Gilroy's estimate that oilservice supplies in Canada is now a $2.5 billion a year business.
But Gilbank stressed that the size of the market and the very definition of what is included in the business varies, and that his estimate was on the liberal side.
"We've been redefining the business," he said.
